notes: LOI third-party enforcement appeal; Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 construction is detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Laemthong Glory: receivers' letter of indemnity enforceable by shipowners under 1999 Act
key_facts: Owners of the vessel Laemthong Glory delivered sugar cargo at Aden without original bills of lading after receiving letters of indemnity from charterers and receivers.
The receivers' LOI was addressed to the charterers, not the owners, but was sent to the owners to procure delivery.
After discharge the vessel was arrested by the Yemen Bank holding the original bills of lading.
The owners sought direct enforcement of the receivers' LOI for indemnity and security under the 1999 Act.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Cooke J's declaration that owners could enforce the receivers' LOI directly under section 1 of the 1999 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; owners were entitled to enforce clauses 1 and 3 of the receivers' LOI as third-party beneficiaries.
enrichment.ratio: Where receivers request charterers to deliver cargo through shipowners as agents and agree to indemnify 'you, your servants and agents', the owners fall within the LOI as agents of the charterers and may enforce indemnity and security clauses under section 1(1)(b) of the 1999 Act; a chain of LOIs is not analogous to construction sub-contract chains for section 1(2) purposes.
legal_issues: Whether LOI terms purported to confer a benefit on the shipowners within section 1(1)(b)
Whether 'agents' in the LOI extended to the owners delivering cargo
Whether indemnity clauses applied only to losses sustained by the charterers
Whether parties intended third-party enforceability despite a chain of LOIs
linked_authorities: Nisshin Shipping Co Ltd v Cleaves & Co Ltd [2003] EWHC 2602 (Comm)
Law Commission Report No 242

confidence.notes: Statutory construction, LOI terms and appellate reasoning on both section 1 issues are explicit.

notes: Unsafe convictions appeal; septic tank manslaughter and section 37 HSWA neglect analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Kelly and Frear: unsafe convictions after child fell into caravan site septic tank

statutes_considered.title: Health and Safety at Work Act 1974

key_facts: Four-year-old Nathan Pringle fell through an insecure septic tank cover at Newperran caravan site in Cornwall and drowned.
Mr Kelly, the site manager, was convicted of gross negligence manslaughter; Mr Frear, a director with overall health and safety responsibility, of criminal neglect under section 37.
Critical evidence on cover seating was destroyed when remedial works were ordered before expert examination.
The trial judge later expressed difficulty reconciling her sentencing remarks with the jury's verdicts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge in manslaughter and section 37 Health and Safety at Work Act proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; both convictions quashed as unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: Where prosecution evidence as to manhole cover condition and seating at the material time was destroyed and sparse, and the judge did not focus the jury on the critical particulars of gross negligence or criminal neglect, convictions for manslaughter and section 37 neglect cannot safely stand despite a prima facie case at the close of the prosecution.
legal_issues: Whether failure to preserve scene evidence rendered trial unfair
Whether there was sufficient evidence of defective cover seating and appellants' knowledge
Whether section 37 requires something more than failure to recognise a risk
Whether the judge's summing-up adequately directed the jury on critical particulars
linked_authorities: R v Birmingham & Ors [1992] Crim LR 117
R (Ebrahim) v Feltham Magistrates' Court [2001] 2 Cr App R 23

confidence.notes: Grounds of appeal, judge's sentencing remarks and court's explicit unsafety conclusion are clearly recorded.

notes: Sentencing appeal for causing death by dangerous driving; Cooksley guidelines applied in detail.

enrichment.short_title: May: eight-year sentence reduced for causing death by dangerous driving
key_facts: David May, aged 18, drove at 45–51 mph in a 30 mph residential area after drinking and while disqualified from driving.
He lost control on a familiar bend, killed cyclist Mark Lucas instantly, and crashed through patio doors into a house before fleeing the scene.
He had been disqualified for drink-driving only six weeks earlier and had never held a licence or taken lessons.
The Recorder sentenced him to eight years' detention in a YOI and ten years' disqualification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by leave against sentence for causing death by dangerous driving and associated driving whilst disqualified.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; sentence reduced to six-and-a-half years' detention and disqualification to seven years.
enrichment.ratio: Even in the highest culpability category under Cooksley, a double-figure starting point near the new fourteen-year maximum requires careful balancing of aggravating features against youth and guilty plea; an eight-year term after full credit implied too high a starting point.
legal_issues: Whether the judge's starting point was proportionate to culpability under Cooksley
Effect of the increase in maximum sentence from ten to fourteen years
Weight to be given to youth, guilty plea and recent disqualification
Appropriate length of driving disqualification for rehabilitation
linked_authorities: R v Cooksley and Others [2004] 1 Cr App R (S) 1
R v Gray [2005] EWCA Crim (29 April 2005)
R v Corkhill [2002] 2 Cr App R (S) 18

confidence.notes: Facts, guideline analysis and substituted sentence are all clearly stated.

notes: Permission to appeal refused; EAT procedural history on restricted probation dismissal ground.

enrichment.short_title: Yuan v Birkbeck: permission refused on EAT procedural challenge
key_facts: Dr Yuan was dismissed during his probationary period as a post-doctoral research assistant at Birkbeck College.
He claimed breach of contract for pay in lieu of notice and other losses after termination under clause 20.7.3 of the staff handbook.
The employment tribunal largely rejected his claims; the EAT allowed appeal on the clause 20.7.3 issue only and remitted for rehearing.
Dr Yuan sought permission to appeal EAT decisions restricting his appeal to that single ground.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal from two EAT decisions on scope of appeal and remittal after partial success.
enrichment.outcome: Applications dismissed; no real prospect of success on challenging the EAT's restriction to the clause 20.7.3 ground.
enrichment.ratio: Where the EAT president had identified only one ground with reasonable prospect of success and the appellant failed to appeal that ruling in time, later attempts to reopen other grounds before the Court of Appeal are out of time and those claims had no prospect of success in any event.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Justice Burton's May 2004 ruling dismissed all but one ground of appeal
Whether Dr Yuan was out of time to challenge the EAT's procedural restrictions
Whether remaining breach of contract claims had any prospect of success
Scope of permission to appeal from EAT decisions

confidence.notes: Procedural history and refusal of permission are clearly reasoned though underlying merits were not fully retried.

notes: Easement abandonment appeal dismissed; Gotobed v Pridmore principles applied with procedural observations.

enrichment.short_title: CDC2020 v Ferreira: garage right of way not abandoned after hotel redevelopment
key_facts: CDC2020 owned former Excelsior Hotel land at Hove with a right of way over neighbouring land to three garages on a 'pink' plot.
The garages were demolished in the 1960s for police convalescent home car parks accessed via ramps over the garage site.
The claimant rebuilt three garages on the pink land in 2002 and sought to enforce the 1964 right of way.
Mr Ferreira contended the right was abandoned when garages were demolished and ramps constructed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from county court judgment upholding existence and exercisability of a right of way over the defendant's land.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; right of way had not been abandoned.
enrichment.ratio: Abandonment requires a clear intention that neither the dominant owner nor successors will ever again use the easement; demolition of garages followed by unlawful excessive use for car park access does not, without more, manifest permanent abandonment of a right granted for garage use.
legal_issues: Whether the right of way was exercisable only while garages stood on the dominant tenement
Whether demolition and car park ramps showed intention to abandon forever
Whether unlawful excessive use extinguished or suspended the easement
Application of Gotobed v Pridmore abandonment principles
linked_authorities: Gotobed v Pridmore (1970) 115 Sol Jo 78
Graham v Philcox [1984] QB 747
Das v Linden Mews Ltd [2002] EWCA Civ 590

confidence.notes: Abandonment issue and dismissal are clearly reasoned; Brooke LJ's procedural remarks are supplementary.

notes: Contempt committal appeal partly allowed; procedural unfairness reduced 24-month sentence to 12 months.

enrichment.short_title: Symes: contempt sentence halved after unfair committal hearing
key_facts: Robin Symes was committed for 24 months for breaching undertakings and interlocutory orders in partnership asset litigation.
Admitted contempts included false affidavits about Eileen Gray furniture proceeds and unauthorised sale of an Akhenaten statue for $3 million.
The same judge had conducted Norwich Pharmacal proceedings against Symes' former solicitor in his absence.
Symes appeared unrepresented at committal after legal aid refusal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Peter Smith J's committal order for two consecutive terms totalling 24 months' imprisonment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; sentence reduced to 12 months; suspended sentence discharged; unresolved contempts not to be pursued.
enrichment.ratio: A judge who conducts Norwich Pharmacal enquiries likely to illuminate contempt should not hear the committal; failure to assess mitigation after an arranged interview and leaving matters over to circumvent the two-year maximum also vitiate fairness, warranting substantial sentence reduction though committal was inevitable.
legal_issues: Whether the committal hearing was unfair under Article 6
Whether the same judge should have heard Slade Norwich Pharmacal and committal proceedings
Whether leaving alleged contempts unresolved breached Villiers principles
Appropriate reduction for procedural defects and admissions
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference (No 2 of 2001) [2004] 2 AC 72
Villiers v Villiers [1994] 1 WLR 493
Norwich Pharmacal Co Ltd v Customs and Excise Commissioners [1974] AC 133

confidence.notes: Procedural defects, sentence reduction and Villiers analysis are explicit though some privilege issues were not fully resolved.

notes: Planning s.288 appeal allowed; Secretary of State's quantitative need reasoning upheld against Collins J.

enrichment.short_title: Sainsbury's Kidlington: Court of Appeal restores refusal of store extension
key_facts: Sainsbury's sought to expand its out-of-town Kidlington store after local approval was called in by the Secretary of State.
The inspector supported permission but the Secretary of State refused on the ground quantitative need was not established.
Sainsbury's methodology extrapolated spending growth from a 1991 baseline rather than comparing current supply with purchasing power.
Collins J quashed the refusal, holding the decision letter erred on overtrading and was inadequately reasoned.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Secretary of State's appeal under section 288 against quashing of planning refusal for failure to demonstrate quantitative need.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Collins J's judgment set aside and the Secretary of State's refusal restored.
enrichment.ratio: Overtrading above company average indicates qualitative need but not by itself unmet quantitative demand in a catchment area; a decision-maker may reject non-conventional need evidence if intelligibly explained as failing to show current disequilibrium between local spending power and retail provision.
legal_issues: Whether overtrading could be treated as an indicator of quantitative need
Whether paragraph 15 of the decision letter was adequately reasoned
Whether the Secretary of State could reject Sainsbury's 1991-baseline methodology
Application of PPG6 and the McNulty statement on quantitative need
linked_authorities: South Buckinghamshire DC v Porter (No 2) [2004] UKHL 33
R v Derbyshire CC, ex p Woods [1997] JPL 958

confidence.notes: Decision letter construction and appellate reversal of Collins J are carefully reasoned though paragraph 15 is acknowledged as not readily intelligible.

notes: Brief costs-only judgment; limited substantive ratio but orders on trial and appeal costs are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Black v Davies: costs orders after partial success on copper fraud appeal
key_facts: This judgment follows the substantive appeal in Black v Davies concerning fraudulent Alcatel representations in copper futures trading.
The Court of Appeal had partly allowed Mr Davies' appeal, reversing key findings on timing of instructions to close out positions.
The court had dismissed the cross-appeal on compound interest in deceit damages.
Remaining issues included costs of trial, appeal and a freezing order assessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplementary judgment on costs and remittal following partial allowance of appeal in deceit proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: No order as to trial costs; interest appeal dismissed with costs; Black parties to pay 60% of Davies' other appeal costs; freezing order damages assessment remitted to High Court.
enrichment.ratio: Where both parties had mixed success and the trial involved findings of dishonest conduct affecting credibility, no order as to trial costs may be appropriate; partial appellate success warrants apportionment of appeal costs rather than an all-or-nothing order.
legal_issues: Appropriate costs order at trial given findings of dishonest conduct
Apportionment of appeal costs where each side succeeded on some grounds
Whether the court should determine freezing order damages assessment
Permission to appeal to the House of Lords
linked_authorities: Black v Davies [2005] EWCA Civ 531

confidence.notes: Costs orders are explicit but the judgment contains little independent substantive analysis.

notes: Copper futures deceit appeal; detailed fact reversal on 9 October timing and compound interest analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Black v Davies: deceit damages set aside after transcript analysis
key_facts: Herbert Black traded copper futures through Brandeis Brokers and claimed Mr Davies fraudulently told him Alcatel would deliver 80,000 tonnes to the LME.
Black alleged he instructed closure of his short position on 8 October 1996 but reversed course after Davies' 9 October misrepresentation.
Recorded telephone conversations on 9 October were inconsistent with a firm decision to close out all positions.
Buckley J awarded about $20 million beyond the $48 million recovered from Brandeis; compound interest was refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from trial judgment for damages in deceit and from refusal of compound interest.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; damages award set aside for failure to prove 8–9 October timing; cross-appeal on compound interest dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Contemporaneous taped conversations are the safest starting point for reconstructing trading instructions seven years later; where they show no firm decision to close out on 8 October and no sudden reversal requiring Alcatel information on 9 October, deceit damages exceeding the Brandeis settlement cannot stand; equitable compound interest is limited to fraud cases where money was obtained and retained.
legal_issues: Whether Black gave instructions to close out on the evening of 8 October 1996
Whether Davies provided false Alcatel information on the morning of 9 October
Whether causation was broken by events on 6 November 1996
Whether compound interest is available on common law deceit damages
linked_authorities: Black v Sumitomo Corporation [2002] 1 WLR 1562
Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale v Islington LBC [1996] AC 669
President of India v La Pintada Compania Navigacion SA [1985] AC 104

confidence.notes: Detailed transcript analysis, reversal of key findings and compound interest ruling are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: VAT input tax appeal allowed; supply-to-whom analysis under section 24 VATA 1994 is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Jeancharm: no VAT input credit on employee's criminal defence legal costs
key_facts: Company employee Damian Collins killed two people while driving a company car on a social journey and pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving.
Insurers paid about £95,000 for his defence under a Business Carshield policy; the company paid £16,625 VAT on solicitors' fees.
The company sought to reclaim the VAT as input tax; the VAT Tribunal allowed the claim relying on a BIA practice note.
The policy indemnified permitted drivers directly, not the company, for defence costs under section 148(7).
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by HMRC against VAT Tribunal decision allowing input tax recovery on legal defence costs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Tribunal decision set aside; company not entitled to input tax credit.
enrichment.ratio: Input tax under section 24(1) requires a supply of services to the taxable person who paid the consideration; where insurers instruct and pay solicitors to defend a permitted driver under a direct indemnity conferred by section 148(7), the legal services are not supplied to the employer company even if it pays the VAT element.
legal_issues: Whether solicitors' services were supplied to the company or to the employee/insurer
Whether the tribunal erred in focusing on the purpose of purchasing the insurance policy
Application of Redrow to insurance-funded legal services
Whether legal services were used for the company's business purposes
linked_authorities: Customs & Excise Commissioners v Redrow Group plc [1999] STC 161
Customs & Excise Commissioners v Rosner [1994] STC 228
Flockton Developments Ltd v Customs & Excise Commissioners [1987] STC 394

confidence.notes: To-whom analysis, Redrow distinction and section 148(7) effect are clearly reasoned; purpose question left open.
